notes: The telegrams are only said to come from far-apart towns, so the joke that they arrive at the same time is lost. Optional: after "These towns were very far from each other." add "But the telegrams came at the same time!"
"The elephant stayed in a big house." A big building or a barn would suit an elephant better, but a reader will not stumble on this.
Grammar stays in present and past simple (plus the modal 'can'). No blocking vocabulary beyond the glossed words: 'paper' (newspaper) and 'We are close now' are clear from context.

Quiz Q1 "Why did the elephant rest near New York for two weeks?" has the keyed answer "It needed rest", which repeats the question. Better: "Why did the elephant stay near New York for two weeks?" keyed to "It was tired after the long trip" (and change the sentence in the text to match).

"Some telegrams came from towns very far from each other. But a few of them arrived at the same time." 'But' is a slightly odd connector here; "And a few of them arrived at the same time!" shows the absurdity more clearly.
"The reward grew bigger and bigger." The text never says who raised it. That is fine, but "Blunt made the reward bigger and bigger" would be clearer.
"Somebody took the elephant away during the night!" 'Had taken' is more natural. B1 allows the past perfect, so this could be "Somebody had taken the elephant away during the night!"
"He even put notes in the newspapers for the thieves." 'Messages' or 'notices' is more idiomatic than 'notes'.
There are no conditionals and no passive voice. The level fits.

Faithful to Twain: the 19-foot elephant that eats anything, the $25,000 reward doubled twice, the theory about two thieves with one of them in prison, the circus advertising offer, the telegrams that arrive at the same time from far-apart towns, the coded newspaper messages, the discovery in the headquarters basement, the ruined narrator who still admires Blunt.
The prose is genuinely literary and the irony is well kept ("galloped across the country on paper", "dismissed the objection with a wave of his hand"). It is not padded.
Ending softened at every level: in Twain the elephant is found dead in the basement, but here it is asleep. This counts as acceptable softening for a 4+ app and keeps the satire intact.

summary: All five levels tell Twain's satire faithfully, with the main events in the right order, consistent figures across levels and correctly keyed quizzes. The only big change is the alive elephant at the end, which is acceptable softening for 4+. Remaining points are minor polish: a circular A2 quiz question, a few connector and word choices, and A1 leaving out that the telegrams arrive at the same time.
